Introduction

The modern music industry relies heavily on digital streaming platforms, where algorithms continuously analyze massive amounts of audio data to classify, recommend, and organize content. One of the fundamental challenges in this domain is accurately categorizing music into distinct genres based on its acoustic properties. This project focuses on the analysis of the Spotify Tracks dataset1, which contains 114,000 observations across 125 unique genres. The primary objective of this project is to build and evaluate a robust classification model capable of predicting the musical genre of a track using its continuous audio features, such as danceability, energy, acousticness, and tempo.

Problem Statement

This project is a supervised multiclass classification problem aiming to predict the track_genre (125 categories) of Spotify tracks using audio features. Accurately mapping objective acoustic measurements to subjective genres is challenging but essential for modern automated music recommendation systems.
Potential Challenges:
  • High Cardinality: Text features (artists, album_name) cause dimensionality explosion.
  • Multicollinearity: Features like energy and loudness are highly correlated.
  • Skewed Distributions: Features like speechiness are heavily right-skewed.
  • Overlapping Classes: Differentiating 125 acoustically similar genres is difficult.

Dataset Description

The dataset contains 114,000 samples and 21 columns (features). The columns consist of a mix of numeric and categorical data. Numeric features include continuous variables such as danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, valence, tempo, duration_ms, and popularity. Categorical features include text strings such as track_id, artists, album_name, track_name, explicit, and the target variable track_genre.

Target Imbalance

Analysis of the target variable, track_genre, reveals that there are 114 distinct categories. Each category contains exactly 1,000 sample instances. The data is perfectly balanced across all classes.

      geom_density(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.7) +

print(p1)

      geom_density(fill = "salmon", alpha = 0.7) +
      theme_minimal() +
      labs(title = "Density Plot of Speechiness (Right-Skewed)", x = "Speechiness", y = "Density")

cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_features, use = "complete.obs")

corrplot(cor_matrix, 
         method = "color",
         type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         number.cex = 0.8,
         title = "Correlation Heatmap of Audio Features",
         mar = c(0,0,1,0))

Model Selection

Random Forest is selected as the model for this classification task. This tree-based ensemble is highly effective at capturing the complex, non-linear relationships between acoustic features and subjective musical genres. Given the dataset’s complexity—comprising 114,000 samples across 125 distinct target classes—Random Forest is exceptionally well-suited. It naturally handles features with varying numeric scales without requiring extensive standardization. Furthermore, it is intrinsically robust against feature multicollinearity (such as the high correlation between energy and loudness) and effectively mitigates overfitting through its randomized ensemble approach, making it an optimal choice for this high-dimensional acoustic dataset.

Evaluation Metrics

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of our multiclass classification models across 114 genres, the following metrics will be applied:
  • Accuracy: the overall accuracy will be calculated to measure the total proportion of correctly predicted tracks across the entire dataset. It serves as a straightforward, high-level performance indicator.
  • F1-Score: F1-Score will be caculated for each of the 114 genres and then takes the average. This ensures that the model’s performance on every single genre is evaluated equally.
  • Confusion Matrix: a confusion matrix will be generated to visualize the model’s predictions against the true labels.
